summary: Defines OAM messages for MPLS-based transport networks that tell an endpoint about conditions that disrupt service. It creates an OAM channel and messages that signal different failure types. It was later updated by RFC 7214.

plainLanguage.summary: When a cable breaks, the far end should be told quickly. This defines the alarm messages one end sends so the other end knows service is broken.

questions: what is the mpls lock report message
what is the l-flag in mpls fault oam
subtitle: Alarm messages that tell the end points of a transport path why service broke, so they do not raise a storm of alarms.

tldr.problem: When a link or node fails in an MPLS-based transport network, every path riding on it fails too, and each end point raises its own alarm. Operators need to see the real fault, not a storm of knock-on alarms.
tldr.mechanism: A node that detects a fault or an administrative lock in a server layer sends Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) or Lock Report (LKR) messages downstream, inside the affected paths, over a dedicated fault management channel (code point 0x0058).
tldr.outcome: End points can suppress alarms, tell a lock from a fault and, when the Link Down flag is set, switch over faster. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 7214.

today: RFC 6427 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2011. It was later updated by RFC 7214, so read the two together.

sections.title: Why Fault Messages Are Needed
sections.content:
RFC 6427 defines Fault Management (FM) messages for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in MPLS-based transport networks. In traditional transport networks, a circuit such as a T1 line runs through several switches. If any link or node on its path fails, OAM indications are generated, and they can be used to suppress alarms or to activate a backup circuit. MPLS-based transport networks offer equivalent circuits, so they need an equivalent capability.

When a fault hits a server (sub-)layer, FM messages go to the clients of that layer. The clients can then hold back the alarms that the disruption would otherwise trigger. This prevents a storm of alarms and lets operations focus on the actual faulty elements. The RFC is written to meet the MPLS-TP requirements of RFC 5654 and the OAM requirements of RFC 5860. Applicability to other types of LSPs is beyond its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If a power line is cut, every house on it goes dark and each one phones the power company. This RFC lets the company get one call about the cut instead of a thousand about dark houses.

sections.title: Faults, Locks and the Two Messages
sections.content:
The RFC names two classes of service disruptive condition. A fault is the inability of a function to perform a required action, not counting inability due to preventive maintenance, lack of external resources or planned actions. A lock is an administrative status in which only test traffic, if any, and OAM dedicated to the LSP are expected on it. A server-failure is a fault that has lasted long enough that the server layer is considered to have stopped providing its service. For a protected server, that means the working and protection facilities have all suffered faults of the required duration.

Each class has a message. The Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) is generated when a fault is detected in the server layer. Its main purpose is to suppress alarms in the layer above. It SHOULD be sent as soon as the condition is detected, but it MAY be delayed, and MAY be suppressed if protection works very rapidly. The Lock Report (LKR) is generated when a server layer entity is administratively locked. It suppresses alarms and lets clients tell a lock from a fault.

Intermediate nodes where a client LSP is switched generate these messages. They insert them into the affected client LSPs, downstream of the fault, and repeat them periodically until the condition clears.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of news. One says something broke by accident, the other says someone switched it off on purpose. The message tells the others which one it is.

sections.title: Link Down Indication and Propagation
sections.content:
The Link Down Indication (LDI) is carried by setting the L-Flag to 1 in an AIS message. A node MUST NOT set the L-Flag until the fault is determined to be a server-failure, and MUST set it once it is. For example, during a server layer protection switch the L-Flag stays clear. If the switch does not restore the link within the expected repair time, the node MUST set it. Any hold-off timer on loss of continuity (LOC) must expire first.

A receiver MAY treat an AIS with the L-Flag set as equivalent to LOC at the client layer. Where the Continuity Check (CC) runs at a high rate, to detect failures within tens of milliseconds, the L-Flag MAY be ignored and AIS is used only for alarm suppression. Where CC runs much more slowly, the LDI enables faster switch-over. Receiving an LKR can likewise be treated as loss of continuity.

LSPs can be nested. If the CC function is disabled for the server LSP, a node SHOULD generate AIS toward its clients when either AIS or LKR is raised. The L-Flag is not automatically propagated; the same server-failure rule applies.
sections.plainLanguage: A flag on the message means it is really broken and not just being fixed. Listeners can either ignore the flag or jump to the backup road right away.

sections.title: The Fault Channel and Message Format
sections.content:
FM messages travel in-band of the client LSP or multi-segment pseudowire, behind an Associated Channel Header (ACH). For LSPs that are not pseudowires, the ACH is identified by the Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) from RFC 5586. The Fault Management channel has its own Associated Channel Type, 0x0058. It does not use ACh TLVs and MUST NOT include the ACh TLV header.

The message itself has a version (currently 1), a reserved field, a Message Type (1 for AIS, 2 for LKR, 0 reserved), a flags byte, a Refresh Timer, a Total TLV Length and optional TLVs. Two flags are defined. The L-Flag is the Link Down Indication; it only means something in AIS, and in LKR it MUST be zero and ignored on receipt. The R-Flag is clear to show a fault condition and set to one to show that a previously sent condition has been removed. The Refresh Timer is the maximum time in seconds between successive messages, from 1 to 20; 0 is not permitted. Reserved bits MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.

Two TLVs are defined. The Interface Identifier (IF_ID) TLV has type 1 and length 8, and carries a node identifier and interface number from RFC 6370. The Global Identifier TLV has type 2 and length 4.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a small card with a few boxes: what kind of news, a flag or two, and how often to repeat it. It rides in a special lane so nobody mistakes it for ordinary traffic.

sections.title: Sending, Clearing and Receiving
sections.content:
To signal a condition, a node sets the message type and a Refresh Timer. The timer value MUST NOT change between messages about the same incident. The default is one second if the optional clearing procedure is not used, and 20 seconds if it is. A Global_ID MAY be included. If R-Flag clearing is used, the IF_ID TLV MUST be included; otherwise it MAY be. After the first message, the node MUST send it two more times at one-second intervals, then continue at the Refresh Timer rate until the condition clears.

When a fault clears, the node MUST stop sending the messages. The indication then clears after 3.5 times the Refresh Timer. To clear faster, the node sends the same message with the R-Flag set to one, immediately and then twice more at one-second intervals. If another fault occurs, it MUST stop these and send new messages.

A receiving end point (MEP) ignores messages with a reserved or unknown type, or an unknown version. With the R-Flag at zero, it enters the condition if it is not already in it, or treats the message as a refresh, and in both cases it sets an expiration timer to 3.5 times the Refresh Timer. With the R-Flag at one, it clears the condition matching the message type and IF_ID, and otherwise ignores the message. If the timer expires, the condition is cleared.

At a minimum, an implementation MUST send AIS and LKR once per second, support setting the L-Flag for a server-failure, and receive messages with any allowed Refresh Timer. Other timer values, receiving the L-Flag, both uses of the R-Flag and all TLVs are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The alarm keeps repeating like a doorbell until the problem is fixed. If the doorbell stops ringing for long enough, the listener decides the trouble is over. A special all-clear ring can end it sooner.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MPLS-TP builds on the MPLS security model, which assumes it is very hard to inject traffic into a network. This protocol depends on the security of the Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) itself. A known concern is that the G-ACh can provide a covert channel; it SHOULD NOT be policed by transit nodes.

Spurious fault OAM messages could be used for denial of service. Because the messages are in a control channel, an attacker normally needs access to a node providing the service, and transport networks are usually run as a walled garden. One exception exists: if external MPLS traffic is mapped to an LSP through a penultimate hop pop (PHP) operation, a GAL followed by a fault message could be inserted. Operators SHOULD filter fault OAM messages that have the GAL at the top of the label stack.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone sending fake alarms could cause trouble, but they would normally need to get inside the network first. At the one edge where outsiders could sneak a message in, operators should check the door.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: IANA assigned 0x0058 (Fault OAM, no TLV follows) from the Pseudowire Associated Channel Types registry. It also created three sub-registries under the MPLS OAM Parameters registry. Message Types run 0 to 255: 0 to 251 by Standards Action, 252 to 255 for Experimental Use. The flag space is bits 0 to 7, all by Standards Action, with the L-Flag at bit 6 (0x2) and the R-Flag at bit 7 (0x1). TLV types run 0 to 255: 0 to 191 by Standards Action, 192 to 247 by Specification Required, and 248 to 255 for Experimental Use.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers used in the messages are written in an official list so nobody uses the same number for two different things.

fields.name: Resvd
fields.desc: Reserved; zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Msg Type
fields.desc: 1 is AIS, 2 is LKR, 0 is reserved.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: L-Flag (Link Down Indication) and R-Flag (removal of a condition).

fields.name: Total TLV Len
fields.desc: Total length in bytes of all TLVs that follow.

items.label: AIS
items.desc: Alarm Indication Signal; fault in the server layer.

items.label: LKR
items.desc: Lock Report; server layer entity administratively locked.

items.label: L-Flag
items.desc: Link Down Indication; meaningful only in AIS.

items.label: R-Flag
items.desc: Set to remove a previously sent condition.
